extracted.intended_audience: princes, courtiers, tutors of nobility, and readers of conduct literature
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for educating and advising a prince and for the conduct of a Courtier: what qualities, institutions, and behaviours make a good prince and stable polity, and how a courtier should instruct or shape a prince toward virtue and effective rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding justly and fittingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Command consists in commanding (justly and in those ways that are fitting) reasonable things and those wherein they have authority, and in requiring the same of such men as have in reason to obey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Princes ought often to see with their own eyes and be present at the execution of their commands, and sometimes take part themselves according to the time and need; command is the chief office of princes and those who know how to command are always obeyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish laws to secure peace and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The good prince's office is to establish his people under such laws and ordinances that they may live at ease and peace, without danger and with dignity, and may worthily enjoy tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many states prosper in war but perish in peace for failing to be well established to live at peace; laws and ordinances of justice should be directed to this end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit war aims to defence and just causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes ought not to make their people warlike for lust of rule, but for the sake of being able to defend themselves and their people, to drive out tyrants, or to govern rightly those who were ill-used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training for endless conquest is unreasonable; warlike virtues should be cultivated for defence and just public ends, not for spoils or domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use laws to punish to prevent disorder, not from hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and ordinances of justice ought to punish the wicked, not from hatred, but in order that they may not be wicked and to prevent disturbance of the tranquillity of the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is instrumental to public tranquillity and should be administered to secure peace and correct behaviour rather than for vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate virtues especially suited to war and peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues useful in war include true courage, steadfastness, and enduring patience; justice, continence, and temperance are always fitting, and are needed more in peace and ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosperity and ease easily corrupt; therefore temperance and moral virtues must be exercised especially during peace to prevent intemperance and injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin moral education with habit/practice, then reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral worth is perfected by practice: first teach through habit to govern unreasoning appetites and direct them toward the good; next establish virtues through understanding and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unreasoning part of the soul and appetites precede reason (as seen in children), so early habituation is required, followed by intellectual instruction to make virtues fully fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care for the body early, with view to soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Care must be taken of the body earlier than of the soul, and of the appetite earlier than of reason, but always with a view to perfecting the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes proper timing for marriage, physical exercises, and education from birth to make children handsome, strong and sturdy— bodily conditioning supports moral and intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a mixed council of nobles and popular representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should choose from his subjects a number of the noblest and wisest gentlemen to consult on everything and give them authority; also choose men of lower rank for a popular council to communicate with the nobles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forms a united body that combines Monarchy, Optimates, and People; the prince should preserve demeanor so ministers can speak freely and truth will be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint wise, well-tried men to administer justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the cares of the prince, the most important is that of justice; wise and well-tried men should be chosen to office whose foresight is true foresight accompanied by goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If goodness is lacking, legal skill and subtlety lead to ruin; the guilt of bad appointments falls on the prince who put them in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine true religion with human foresight
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should love God above all and direct his actions to Him as the true end; divine piety combined with human foresight brings good fortune and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be truly religious but not superstitious—avoid incantations and soothsaying; piety helps in prosperity and in seeking mercy in adversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love and balance treatment of land and people
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince ought to love his land and people—neither holding them in excessive bondage nor allowing too much freedom; maintain equality in justice and liberty and judicious inequality in rewards according to merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making oneself odious by oppression or despised by over-freedom; distribute honours and rewards proportional to merits so subjects both love and revere him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a mean in wealth distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wholesome to have the greater part of citizens neither very rich nor very poor; men of moderate fortune do not lay snares for others and form the most powerful body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive riches often cause ruin and exposure to foreign domination; preserving a middle condition in society reduces conspiracy and sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent unrest by rewarding good and precluding bad from power
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid desires for change of government, the prince should win the people's love and obedience by benefiting and rewarding the good and preventing the bad and seditious from becoming powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention is easier before bad actors become powerful; keep subjects from creeping evils and corrupt practices that infect cities slowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide material and moral conditions for subjects' tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should contrive to keep his subjects in a tranquil state and give them blessings of mind, body and fortune so they can exercise the virtues of the mind which are more profitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material well-being (body/fortune) enables the exercise of intellectual virtues; a well-governed people makes the prince a great lord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inculcate regal grandeur tempered by amiability
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should show a certain greatness and regal splendour, readiness of mind and unconquered valour, accompanied by familiar gentleness, amiable humanity and discriminating affection according to merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve majesty suited to rank to avoid over-condescension that lowers authority or sternness that excites hatred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous, splendid, and a patron of public life
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince ought to be very generous and splendid: give magnificent banquets, festivals, games, public shows; keep excellent horses, falcons, hounds and other things pertaining to pleasures of great lords and the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity fosters love and fame; God is said to be the treasurer of generous princes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erect public buildings to win honour and memorialize rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage great public buildings both to win honour in lifetime and to give a memorial of himself to posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: palaces, churches, streets and Roman remains—public works testify to the worth of rulers and secure lasting fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage war against tyrants and for noble causes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fitting to wage perpetual and deadly war against cruel and impious tyrants; extirpation of tyrants is a public benefit deserving of great reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just wars (including those to convert or subjugate infidels, as the text discusses) can be profitable both to vanquishers and vanquished if they bring higher customs and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form virtues genuinely, not merely externals
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues must be internalized—if a prince does not know or has not formed his mind after the pattern of virtue, he will hardly know how to be magnanimous, generous, just, courageous, or foreseeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External acts (building, giving) are insufficient without inner formation; virtues must avoid vices of excess or deficiency and be guided by foresight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern with prudence to find the mean between extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use foresight to detect the central point of virtue between two extremes (vices of excess and deficiency); withdraw step by step opposite to the extreme one is inclined toward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affectations (too affable = despised; too austere = hated; excessive eloquence = weariness). Practice corrective moderation as one straightens crooked timbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to small details and supervise ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confide all control to one minister; the prince should understand acts, be overseer of ministers, settle disputes, make peace, ally subjects in marriage, and promote artisans and merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No man is apt for all things; greater harm springs from credulity than from incredulity. The prince should set limits upon private superfluities (houses, feasts, dowries, luxury) which can ruin cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select ministers prudently and value prudent distrust
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need for the prince to have good judgment to perceive who deserves to be believed; credulity leads to harm whereas measured incredulity can be advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prince must be the overseer of his ministers and not trust any single person with all control; choose and test officials for both ability and goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit private superfluities to preserve public order
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate superfluities by setting limits on sumptuous houses, feasts, excessive doweries, luxury and display in jewels and vesture of private folk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luxury among private citizens causes waste, envy, and moral corruption, sometimes driving women to dishonour for trinkets; moderation protects the commonwealth.
